name: bzip2 0.6 (libbz2-rs-sys Rust backend)
baseline: The C libbzip2 that the bzip2 crate linked through bzip2-sys before 0.6.0
verdict_reason: The Rust port needs 9.66% to 14.87% fewer CPU cycles to compress and 4.48% to 10.00% fewer to decompress across the published inputs. Since bzip2 0.6.0 it is the crate's default, so upgrading gets the gain.
tier_reason: First-party CPU-cycle counts with no machine, compiler or flags stated.
claimed_speedup: Compression: -14.87% CPU cycles (sample3.ref), -14.30% (silesia-small.tar level 1), - 9.66% (level 9); decompression: - 4.48% to -10.00% CPU cycles across six files.
workload: Compress sample3.ref and silesia-small.tar at levels 1 and 9; decompress six .bz2 files from 2.5M to 2.3G cycles of work.
platforms: Any Rust target, including wasm32 and Windows without a C toolchain
install: cargo add bzip2 (0.6.0 or later uses the Rust backend by default)
one_liner: bzip2 crate 0.6 swapped C libbzip2 for a Rust port: 10-15% fewer cycles to compress, 4-10% fewer to decompress.
how_it_is_fast: libbz2-rs-sys started as a c2rust translation of libbzip2 and was then cleaned up and tuned with the lessons from zlib-rs. The post does not break down which changes produced the gain.
use_it_when: You already depend on bzip2 (often indirectly through zip or tar crates): upgrading to 0.6 gets the speedup
You need bzip2 on wasm or cross-compiled targets where building C is a problem
skip_it_when: You need byte-identical behavior with a system libbzip2 shared library for some external reason
caveats: Cycle counts, not wall time; the post does not name the machine and notes noisier decompression results on its macOS benchmark machine
First-party numbers with no CPU named
tradeoffs: Contains unsafe code to mirror the C interface; tested under Miri and audited by Radically Open Security
libbz2-rs-sys is distributed under the bzip2-1.0.6 license, while the bzip2 crate is MIT OR Apache-2.0

evidence.quote: which uses our rust implementation of the bzip2 algorithm
Our rust implementation generally outperforms the C implementation, though there are a couple of cases where we only match C performance.
